one_liner: Hash and password-KDF functions in C compiled to tiny wasm modules; 1.5-16x faster than the best pure-JS libraries tested.
what_it_does: Provides about 25 hash functions for browsers, Node.js and Deno (MD4/MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2, SHA-3, Keccak, BLAKE2b/2s/3, xxHash32/64/3/128, CRC32/CRC64, Adler-32, RIPEMD-160, SM3, Whirlpool) plus HMAC, PBKDF2, scrypt, bcrypt and Argon2. There are two API shapes: promise-returning one-shot functions such as md5(data) that return hex, and createXXX() hashers with synchronous init/update/digest and save()/load() of the internal state for resumable hashing. Inputs can be strings (hashed as UTF-8), Buffers or typed arrays; the API resembles Node's createHash but is not call-compatible with crypto-js, spark-md5 or noble-hashes.
how_it_is_fast: Each algorithm is portable scalar C (for example Solar Designer's public-domain MD5 and an RHash-style SHA-256 with rounds fully unrolled by #pragma clang loop unroll(full)) compiled freestanding with clang -O3 -flto into its own wasm module of a few kB with a fixed 128 KiB memory. Input is copied into a 16 KiB staging buffer in linear memory and hashed chunk by chunk; for inputs under 16 KiB the shorthand functions run init, update and final in a single JS-to-wasm call and format hex into a preallocated buffer. The largest gains are on 64-bit-word algorithms (SHA3-512 16.5x over noble-hashes, xxHash64 378x over xxhashjs, which emulates 64-bit math), consistent with wasm's native i64 arithmetic; there is no WASM SIMD or threading (the README lists both as future plans).
when_to_use: Browser or Deno code hashing large in-memory buffers or file chunks with algorithms that WebCrypto's digest() does not provide, such as MD5, xxHash, BLAKE2/BLAKE3, CRC32/CRC64 or SHA-3 (MD5 850 MB/s vs spark-md5 172 MB/s at 1 MB).
Streaming or resumable hashing: synchronous update()/digest() inside a worker, or save()/load() to split hashing of a big file across invocations.
Password hashing in a JS runtime without native bindings: Argon2id 438 vs 213 ops/s for argon2-browser, PBKDF2-SHA512 588 vs 395 ops/s for noble-hashes, plus bcrypt and scrypt.
Many tiny inputs where per-call cost matters: the shorthand path reached 110 MB/s on 32-byte MD5 inputs vs 39 MB/s for spark-md5.
Bundle-size-sensitive apps: each algorithm is a separate tree-shakable module of 3-11 kB gzipped.
when_not_to_use: SHA-1/SHA-2 where crypto.subtle.digest or node:crypto createHash is available: neither native path is in the author's benchmark, user-submitted MeasureThat.net runs (search snippets only; the pages were unreachable) show WebCrypto SHA-256 at roughly 2-4x hash-wasm's ops/s, and issue #47 reports hash-wasm about 9x slower than crypto.subtle with Chrome DevTools open.

Pages with a strict Content-Security-Policy that lacks 'unsafe-eval' or 'wasm-unsafe-eval': WebAssembly.compile of the embedded base64 module fails (issue #3, open; the maintainer declined an injectable WebAssembly option).
xxHash64 on large inputs as the only need: hash-wasm and xxhash-wasm are level at 1 MB (15,989 vs 15,929 MB/s).

Fastest possible Argon2, or Argon2 with parallelism above 1: the sibling @phi-ag/argon2 measures 1.68-2.07x hash-wasm's Argon2, and hash-wasm's lib/argon2.ts fills the lanes one after another in a single wasm instance, so extra lanes add no speed (multithreading is only a README future plan).
Long-lived Firefox pages that hash thousands of files or call argon2id repeatedly: several users report memory growth until out-of-memory (issue #69, open, not reproduced on Node or Chromium).

integration.dependencies: none (each wasm binary is embedded as base64 in its JS module)
integration.min_toolchain: Chrome 57+, Safari 11+, Firefox 53+, Edge 16+, Node.js 8+, Deno 1+ per the README; rebuilding the wasm needs Docker with Alpine's clang and lld (alpine:3.20.3 at HEAD)
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly host (wasm32 scalar code, no SIMD); not Internet Explorer
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded JS API: one-shot functions share one cached wasm instance per algorithm, createXXX() hashers hold separate state; usable in Web Workers with one set of instances per worker

gotchas: Harness details behind the README tables (author's hash-wasm-benchmark app): it measures both the shorthand md5() and createMD5() variants but the README shows one hash-wasm row per table without saying which; the xxhash-wasm row wraps h64Raw in an async function inside addSync and allocates a Buffer and a BigInt per call, which inflates hash-wasm's 2.1x lead at 32 bytes; bench.js addAsync batches calls as Promise.all([array]), so the batch is never awaited (harmless here because these libraries finish their work synchronously or in microtasks, but it would mis-time a truly asynchronous function such as WebCrypto); the SHA3-512 table labels jsSHA 3.2.0 although the app pins jssha 3.3.1. The tables measure the npm 4.10.0 build, not the shipped 4.12.0.
Strings are hashed as their UTF-8 bytes with no normalisation, so visually equal strings (precomposed vs combining characters) hash differently; normalize() first, as the README advises.

One-shot functions return Promises even though the work is synchronous once the module is cached; createXXX() instantiates a new wasm module each call, so call it once and reuse it with init() rather than creating hashers in a loop.

save() output contains plaintext input bytes and is tagged with a hash of the exact wasm build, so load() throws across hash-wasm versions; users report Chrome running hash-wasm roughly 9-10x slower while DevTools is open (issue #47, open).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick hash-wasm when one dependency must cover many algorithms, from MD5 to Argon2, with streaming and resumable state; pick xxhash-wasm when xxHash alone is needed (equal at 1 MB), @phi-ag/argon2 for faster Argon2, and awasm-noble or blake3-jit when BLAKE3 throughput is the only concern, since hash-wasm publishes no BLAKE3 number.
verified_claims_summary: Author's in-browser benchmark (hash-wasm-benchmark app, Chrome 131 on a Ryzen 9 7900X, hash-wasm 4.10.0 built with clang -O3 -flto in Alpine 3.18.4, every library's digest checked against hash-wasm's during warm-up, about 1 s per scenario): at 1 MB MD5 850 MB/s vs spark-md5 172 (4.95x), SHA-256 426 vs noble-hashes 1.3.2 110 (3.9x), SHA3-512 234 vs 14.2 (16.5x), xxHash64 15,989 vs xxhashjs 42 MB/s but level with xxhash-wasm; PBKDF2-SHA512 588 vs 395 ops/s for noble-hashes (1.49x) and Argon2id 438 vs 213 ops/s for argon2-browser (2.06x), ratios derived from page data. No native WebCrypto or node:crypto baseline was measured.
status_note: Stale since 4.12.0 (2024-11-19) with 9 open issues (Firefox memory growth #69, CSP #3, a WASM SIMD request #66), but MIT-licensed, dependency-free, 1.2k stars and small per-algorithm modules, so it is a safe pick for hashing in JS runtimes when native crypto is unavailable or lacks the algorithm.
